true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check is not atomic with insert

CreateOrUpdateDevice counts active rows and, only if count < deviceLimit, runs a separate INSERT. Those steps are not in one transaction and take no lock, so concurrent anonymous logins can all observe the same count below the cap and all insert. The configured limit can be exceeded under parallel traffic (multiple Grafana instances make this worse). Enforce the cap in the same transaction as the insert, or with a row/advisory lock, so the count and write cannot race.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device-limit denial is cached, so a retry bypasses the limit

tagDeviceUI writes the device key into localCache before CreateOrUpdateDevice returns. When the store rejects a new device with ErrDeviceLimitReached, that key stays cached for the default 29 minutes and the error is returned only for the current call. Authenticate treats that error as a hard failure, but the next anonymous request for the same X-Grafana-Device-Id hits the cache, returns nil, and is issued an anonymous identity without ever being inserted or counted. Refreshing once therefore bypasses the configured device limit, and those sessions never appear in the 30-day count, so the cap stays artificially low. Clear the cache entry (or set it only after a successful write) when tagging fails.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
New auth.anonymous device_limit setting is undocumented

AnonymousDeviceLimit is read from [auth.anonymous] device_limit (default 0 = unlimited) but this PR does not add the key to conf/defaults.ini or the auth configuration docs. Operators have no documented name, default, or meaning for the limit, so the feature cannot be configured from the shipped sample config.

Wire provider signature changed but generated injector was not updated

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService no longer accepts anonstore.AnonStore and now requires db.DB, and ProvideAnonDBStore gained a deviceLimit argument. Grafana constructs this service from the checked-in Wire injector (pkg/server/wire_gen.go), which is not in this PR. The existing injector still calls the old signature, so the OSS server package will not compile until wire is regenerated and any other call sites are updated.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup debug logs left at Error level with full ID lists

CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags call r.log.Error on every batch (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579), including the successful path where err is nil. Each line dumps the full ids slice and the SQL condition. With a configured batch size in the tens of thousands this writes enormous error-level log records on every cleanup cycle even when nothing is wrong, flooding logs and adding allocation/IO cost to the job the PR is trying to make safer. These should be removed or reduced to debug without the ID list.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker shortened from 10 minutes to 1 minute

Run now starts the background cleanup ticker at 1 minute instead of 10. Nothing in the PR description or the deadlock fix requires this, and it looks like leftover debugging next to the new Error logs. clean() uses a 9-minute timeout and runs synchronously, while time.Ticker buffers one tick, so a job longer than a minute will be re-entered immediately and the whole cleanup suite (annotations, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, invites, short URLs, query history) can run nearly continuously. That multiplies database load and can recreate the write contention this change is meant to avoid.

false_positives.candidate:
SQLite ID list built with quadratic string concatenation

When the SQLite fallback inlines IDs because AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize exceeds 999, deleteByIDs grows the IN-list with fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) on every element. That copies the whole string each iteration. The new integration test exercises this path with a batch of 32767, so a single DELETE statement build is quadratic in the batch size and can stall the cleanup goroutine for a large annotation table. Build the list with strings.Builder or strings.Join instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Storage failures and legacy delete-collection are recorded on the wrong metric series

On Storage.Create failure the code calls recordLegacyDuration (line 45) instead of recordStorageDuration; Storage.Update failure does the same at line 129. Successful Delete records the object name as the kind label (line 106: recordStorageDuration(..., name, ...)) instead of options.Kind, so the kind cardinality is object names. The legacy DeleteCollection goroutine calls recordStorageDuration (line 166) rather than recordLegacyDuration, so legacy latency and errors are attributed to unified storage. Mode 3 dashboards and alerts will mis-attribute failures and cannot tell whether the safety write succeeded.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled when the handler returns

Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine via context.WithTimeoutCause on the incoming request context (lines 51, 110, 135, and 163). That child context is cancelled as soon as the apiserver finishes the request and cancels the parent, which is normally before the 10s timeout. The legacy write that mode 3 is supposed to perform as a safety copy therefore fails immediately with context canceled, so legacy storage silently diverges from unified storage.

Legacy create/update replay the caller's object instead of the unified result

After Storage.Create returns, the goroutine calls Legacy.Create with the same obj pointer the storage implementation just mutated (UID, resourceVersion, timestamps). Legacy.Update (line 139) likewise reuses the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of writing the object Storage.Update already produced. The previous mode 3 update path wrapped that result so both stores stored the same bytes. Legacy optimistic concurrency then sees the unified resourceVersion, rejects or no-ops the write, and the two stores diverge. Failures are not logged, only counted, so the mismatch is invisible.

Mode 3 playlist integration test reads legacy immediately after an async write

The new mode 3 file/unified/etcd cases call doPlaylistTests, which creates, updates, and deletes through the Kubernetes API and then immediately lists and gets the same objects on the legacy /api/playlists endpoints (around lines 522-531 and getFromBothAPIs). Mode 3 only copies to legacy asynchronously and does not wait for that copy, so those assertions race the goroutine and will flake or fail even when the async write would eventually succeed.

Mode 3 unit tests mock the wrong store and never wait for the legacy goroutine

The create/update/delete error cases set expectations on Legacy (or none on Storage) even though the implementation returns the Storage error and only then calls Legacy. An unmocked Storage.Create returns a nil error, so the wantErr cases do not exercise the path they name. Success cases start an unsynchronized goroutine that calls Legacy after the test function returns and never assert that the legacy call happened or that its error was recorded. These tests will flake or panic on the mock after the test ends and do not lock in the dual-write contract.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache fill is not rechecked under the write lock

GetWebAssets snapshots entryPointAssetsCache under a read lock, drops that lock, and only then takes the write lock and always reloads and assigns entryPointAssetsCache. Two callers that both observe a nil cache can both enter the write section. If the first finishes and publishes a good manifest, the second still overwrites it—including with nil when its read fails—so a successful fill is discarded and later non-dev callers miss the cache or all redo the load. After Lock, re-read the cache and return it when non-nil and not in dev, and do not assign a failed result over an existing entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

Cache fill is not rechecked under the write lock

GetWebAssets snapshots entryPointAssetsCache under a read lock, drops that lock, and only then takes the write lock and always reloads and assigns entryPointAssetsCache. Two callers that both observe a nil cache can both enter the write section. If the first finishes and publishes a good manifest, the second still overwrites it—including with nil when its read fails—so a successful fill is discarded and later non-dev callers miss the cache or all redo the load. After Lock, re-read the cache and return it when non-nil and not in dev, and do not assign a failed result over an existing entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
SQL kill-switch reported as invalid SQL

The legacy expression path still builds a SQLCommand via NewSQLCommand, which calls sql.TablesList. That now always fails because pkg/expr/sql/db.go RunCommands returns "not implemented" after DuckDB was removed. NewSQLCommand maps every such failure to a BadRequest (sql-invalid-sql / "error reading SQL command") and logs "invalid sql query". Previously valid SQL expressions are therefore rejected as malformed user SQL, not as a disabled feature. ExpressionQueryReader is a second entry point and returns a different error, "sqlExpressions is not implemented" (pkg/expr/reader.go), while enableSqlExpressions ignores FlagSqlExpressions and always returns false. Clients and the UI cannot tell a security disable (CVE-2024-9264) from a bad query, and the still-documented feature flag does not change either outcome.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
SQL kill-switch reported as invalid SQL

The legacy expression path still builds a SQLCommand via NewSQLCommand, which calls sql.TablesList. That now always fails because pkg/expr/sql/db.go RunCommands returns "not implemented" after DuckDB was removed. NewSQLCommand maps every such failure to a BadRequest (sql-invalid-sql / "error reading SQL command") and logs "invalid sql query". Previously valid SQL expressions are therefore rejected as malformed user SQL, not as a disabled feature. ExpressionQueryReader is a second entry point and returns a different error, "sqlExpressions is not implemented" (pkg/expr/reader.go), while enableSqlExpressions ignores FlagSqlExpressions and always returns false. Clients and the UI cannot tell a security disable (CVE-2024-9264) from a bad query, and the still-documented feature flag does not change either outcome.

false_positives.candidate:
No test that SQL expressions stay disabled

This change removes the DuckDB engine and is meant to close RCE/LFI via SQL expressions, but it adds no test that a SQL expression is rejected on both entry points (ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery and UnmarshalSQLCommand/Execute) and that no query is executed. The only enforcement on the legacy path is a stub whose errors are labeled "not implemented", and enableSqlExpressions is an inverted flag check that happens to return false on every branch. A regression that fills in the stub or "fixes" that helper would restore execution with no CI failure. The PR description records only manual checks.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Same-key index builds no longer serialized

BuildIndex used to hold cacheMu for the whole build, which at least serialized bleve.New and cache publication. The lock is now taken only to assign b.cache[key]. getOrCreateIndex still does check-then-act (GetIndex, then build) with no per-key singleflight, and init can build many namespaces at once. Two callers for the same NamespacedResource can both pass GetIndex, both call bleve.New on the same directory (file indexes fail or corrupt the on-disk index), and the last cache write wins while the other caller keeps using the orphaned index. Searches and watch updates then diverge.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the cache map without the mutex

TotalDocs ranges over b.cache with no cacheMu held, while BuildIndex writes that map under cacheMu. searchSupport.init now starts the watch goroutine (which can BuildIndex a namespace that was below the init threshold) and then calls TotalDocs for the new startup log. A concurrent map write during that iteration panics the process.

false_positives.candidate:
BuildIndex span context is still discarded

The PR's stated trace fix is to pass the span context into child work (`ctx, span := tracer.Start`). BuildIndex, which this change edits, still does `_, span := b.tracer.Start(...)`. The builder callback and SQL list work started from the incoming ctx are not children of the BuildIndex span, so the index-build trace stays disconnected from the work it wraps.

Concurrent index init races on shared err

searchSupport.init launches one errgroup goroutine per namespace and each one does `_, _, err = s.build(...)` plus `totalBatchesIndexed++` on variables declared outside the loop. Those are unsynchronized shared writes. With BuildIndex no longer holding a process-wide lock, these goroutines actually run together, so a failed build can have its error overwritten by a later successful one (startup proceeds with a missing index) or a finished success can be overwritten by another goroutine's error (startup fails spuriously). The counter read for the trace event is likewise racy.

Failed constructor Init leaks lifecycle and in-flight builds

NewResourceServer now calls s.Init and, on error, returns nil without s.cancel() or lifecycle.Stop. Init runs lifecycle.Init (SQL backend opens the DB) before search.init. If index build fails, the caller has no server handle to stop the backend, so the DB pool is leaked. The cancelable context passed into the errgroup is also dropped, so in-flight namespace builds keep running after the constructor has already failed. Previously Init errors were returned on the live server, which could still be stopped.

Search watch loop panics when the event channel closes

After the index build, init always starts `for { v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v) }` on context.Background(), not the server context. WatchWriteEvents' poller closes that channel when the SQL backend is stopped. A receive on a closed channel yields a nil *WrittenEvent, and handleEvent immediately reads evt.Type, which panics. Because init now runs inside NewResourceServer, every storage server starts this goroutine, and shutdown (server.Stop / backend cancel) will crash it. The goroutine also cannot be cancelled independently of the SQL poller.

Storage-server startup test skipped on postgres

TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer is the integration test that constructs and runs a storage-server target, which now builds the unified index inside NewResourceServer/InitializeModuleServer. The change skips that test whenever GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres, with a TODO that it fails in Drone. Postgres startup regressions from eager index init (the failure mode this PR is fixing) will not be caught in CI.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Login-cache test cleanup targets alias "alias"

testCacheIDPForLogin creates idp-alias-0..20 but registers cleanup as testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove (also at the idp-alias-20 create). That resource is not one of the created providers, so the 21 brokers are left in the shared test realm. Later tests that count or list identity providers can fail or see extra login IdPs, and the new assertions never check that the cached ids are the expected aliases rather than only a size.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation uses org-wrapped isEnabled and can skip

update() loads the pre-image with getById(), which returns the organization-aware wrapper whose isEnabled() is false when the IdP is linked to a missing or disabled organization (or when the organization provider is disabled), even if the stored enabled flag is true. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate treats that wrapper as "not a login IdP". If the update also makes the raw model ineligible (enabled=false, hideOnLogin, link-only, or broker-public cleared), both predicate checks fail and the method returns without invalidating the getForLogin list keys. Those lists were built from the JPA enabled/hide/link/public filters, so they still contain the IdP. After the org is enabled again, getForLogin keeps returning it, and OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean only re-checks isEnabled(), not hideOnLogin/linkOnly/broker-public, so a hidden or link-only broker can show up on the login page until some other event drops the cache. Compare against the delegate/raw model (or always invalidate login keys on update).

getForLogin cache drops provider order

Delegate getForLogin results are collected with Collectors.toSet() and then copied into a HashSet before the stream is returned. That discards the stable order previously produced by getAllStream (typically alias or creation order). Login pages sort with a comparator that is usually guiOrder, and the default guiOrder is the same for every broker, so the stable sort keeps HashSet iteration order. Brokers therefore shuffle between requests. Preserve encounter order (for example LinkedHashSet) when caching ids and when building the result stream.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK keystore provider, not BC

getBouncyCastleProvider() returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is the platform keystore provider (typically SunJSSE), not BouncyCastle and not null. Elytron's provider returns null so callers skip BC-specific setup. Callers that do Signature/Cipher.getInstance(alg, provider) with this result look up algorithms only in that provider, which does not implement SHA256withECDSA or the BC padding names Keycloak uses, so ECDSA/JWE operations fail with NoSuchAlgorithmException even though the JDK can perform them. If BouncyIntegration records this provider's name as the crypto provider, later lookups are pinned to the wrong provider for the life of the process.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() is abstract and breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

order() was added as a new abstract method on the public CryptoProvider SPI. Existing compiled implementations that are not in this PR (custom or older provider jars) no longer satisfy the interface. CryptoIntegration.detectProvider instantiates every provider via ServiceLoader and immediately calls order() to sort, so those implementations fail at startup with AbstractMethodError instead of being ignored. A default method (for example returning 0) would keep old providers loadable and still let the new authz provider lose to explicitly higher-order ones.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
ECDSA integer conversion silently truncates oversized components

integerToBytes, used by asn1derToConcatenatedRS, copies the low qLength bytes whenever BigInteger.toByteArray() is longer than the curve field size and never checks that the discarded prefix is a single 0x00 sign byte. A non-canonical or oversized ASN.1 INTEGER is therefore rewritten into a different in-range R or S instead of being rejected. Signature conversion then succeeds with a value that is not the one that was signed, so verification can fail closed only by chance, or accept a rewritten component, instead of raising IOException on malformed DER.

ECDSA tests use one P-256 key and never check JDK verification

The suite generates a single KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC") key, which is P-256, and uses it for ES256, ES384, and ES512. It only asserts that asn1derToConcatenatedRS and concatenatedRSToASN1DER round-trip through this provider's own decoder. It never calls Signature.verify on the DER produced by concatenatedRSToASN1DER, and ES384/ES512 never see 48-byte or 66-byte R/S values from a matching curve. A DER encoding that Java's strict verifier rejects, or a high-bit padding bug that only shows up at the real ES384/ES512 sizes, still passes.

FIPS, Elytron, and default providers share the same order

FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and DefaultCryptoProvider all return order 200, while detectProvider now keeps the first provider after a stable sort instead of failing when more than one CryptoProvider is on the classpath. Equal order preserves ServiceLoader/classpath order, so a deployment that contains both the FIPS provider and the default (or Elytron) provider silently runs whichever jar appears first. That can disable FIPS mode without an error. FIPS needs a strictly higher order than the non-FIPS providers now that multiple providers are allowed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client removal no longer cleans permissions when only V2 is enabled

The removal listener is now skipped unless ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) is enabled. With only V2 enabled, ClientRemovedEvent does not run, and ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled throws anyway, so there is no cleanup of the authz resource named with the deleted client's id. A later permission evaluation can still grant scopes on that orphan id, and resource listings keep growing after clients are deleted.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission returns the type resource name, not client ids

getClientsWithPermission searches resources of type "Clients" and adds resource.getName() for every granted scope. The all-clients resource created by the schema is itself typed "Clients" and named "Clients", so a realm-wide grant inserts the literal "Clients" into the result and does not expand to actual client ids. Callers that filter client lists or role-mapping targets by this set will either hide every real client or treat a non-client id as granted. Per-client resources are only present after a specific permission was created, so an all-clients MAP_ROLES/VIEW grant cannot be applied through this API.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
All-clients fallback NPEs when the Clients resource is missing

hasPermission(ClientModel, String) treats a missing per-client resource as an all-clients check, then calls PolicyStore.findByResource with whatever getResourceTypeResource returns. That helper returns null when the admin-permissions client has no "Clients" resource (schema not initialized, or an already-enabled realm that never received the new type). findByResource(server, null) then throws, so a normal manage/view/configure check becomes a 500 instead of a deny. The same null is later passed into ResourcePermission if the empty-policy guard is skipped.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
Client permission resources are not resolved to a display name

getResourceName now has a Clients resource type whose stored name is the client UUID, but the method only special-cases Users and otherwise returns resource.getDisplayName(). Client resources are created with name set to the internal id and no display name, so admin permission listings show null (or a raw id) instead of the clientId. Deleting or renaming the client also has no equivalent of the user-not-found check, so stale client resources stay unlabeled.

Existing admin-permissions clients never get the Clients type or scopes

init() returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already set, and nothing else in this change creates the new Clients resource or the configure, map-roles-client-scope, and map-roles-composite scopes. Realms that already enabled fine-grained admin permissions V2 therefore keep a schema that only has Users. Creating a Clients permission then fails scope validation ("No scopes found" / "Scope was not found for resource type"), and evaluation cannot fall back to an all-clients resource that was never stored.

V2 client permission hooks throw instead of denying

MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() now always returns ClientPermissionsV2 when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is on, but isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, canExchangeTo, resource, getPermissions, and the Policy accessors throw UnsupportedOperationException. Those methods are on the live admin evaluator path (client removal, permissions UI, token exchange). A caller that previously got false/null from the V1 evaluator now fails the request with 500, including for admins who only have realm roles and never opted into per-client policies.

requireView javadoc describes a boolean return

The new comments on requireView and requireViewClientScopes say they return true when canView()/canViewClientScopes() is true. Both methods are void and are documented elsewhere as throwing ForbiddenException. Implementors and callers reading only these comments will treat a failed check as a boolean instead of an authorization failure.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

false_positives.candidate:
Default update-strategy tests never enable rolling-updates

createInitialDeployment returns immediately when updateStrategy is null, before the new FeatureSpec setup that enables rolling-updates. Both parameterized tests (testImageChange and testCacheMaxCount) include that null case, which is the documented default strategy. The operator guide in this PR states the preview feature must be enabled or the operator fails, so these cases deploy a CR without the feature and will not exercise (or will fail) the default upgrade path the test is meant to cover. Enable the feature before that return so every strategy, including the default, runs with rolling-updates.

Enabling rolling-updates replaces any existing enabled features

setEnabledFeatures(List.of(ROLLING_UPDATES)) overwrites the CR's entire enabled-features list instead of appending. If getTestKeycloakDeployment (or a future caller) already set spec.features.enabled, those features are dropped whenever a non-default UpdateStrategy is applied. The server then starts with a different feature set than the rest of the operator suite, so upgrade assertions can pass or fail for the wrong reason. Add rolling-updates to the existing list rather than replacing it.

Feature-disabled test does not assert exit code 4

testFeatureNotEnabled only checks the error string. This PR makes exit code 4 the contract for a disabled rolling-updates feature (and moves the recreate-upgrade code from 4 to 3). true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Join timeout leaves flusher processes running

SpanFlusher.join() sets the shared stopped flag, spends the entire timeout in next_step.join(), then breaks out of the process loop when remaining_time <= 0 before calling process.terminate(). Unlike the previous single-process join, a timed-out shutdown therefore does not signal or kill any flusher process that is blocked in Redis or Kafka future.result() and has not yet observed stopped. Those processes are not reaped on rebalance (the consumer process stays up; daemon exit only happens when the parent exits), so they keep flushing the same shards while the new assignment starts its own flushers. That races flush_segments/done_flush_segments and produces duplicate segments to the buffered-segments topic.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same bug: breaking out of the loop when the deadline/timeout expires skips calling terminate() on the remaining flusher processes, leaving them running after shutdown.

false_positives.candidate:
Restart starts a second flusher before the first is dead

_ensure_processes_alive() kill()s a hung SpawnProcess and immediately calls _create_process_for_shards without join() or any wait until exitcode is set. SIGKILL is asynchronous, and kill failures are swallowed, so the old process can still be inside flush_segments, produce, or done_flush_segments when the replacement process starts on the same shard list. Two flushers then mutate the same Redis segments and both emit Kafka payloads, duplicating spans. The replaced Process object is also dropped without join(), so each restart leaks a zombie until the consumer exits.

Flusher metric tags embed comma-joined shard lists

shard_tag is ",".join of every shard owned by the process, and it is sent as the statsd/metrics tag shard (and, on wait_produce, shards). With the CLI default of --flusher-processes 1, one process owns every assigned partition, so the tag value is a comma-separated list such as "0,1,2,...". DogStatsD encodes tags as comma-separated key:value pairs, so that value is parsed as extra tags and the timer is dropped or attributed wrong. It also makes the series cardinality depend on the partition assignment instead of a single shard id, and the same string is set as a Sentry SDK tag that will exceed the 200-character tag limit on large assignments.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

Kafka commits are issued from a background thread

close() stops the commit thread before pool.shutdown(). shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True and then shuts the queues down. Those offsets stay outstanding, and because the commit thread has already been joined they are never committed. join() also ignores the timeout argument and close() joins each worker for up to 5s sequentially, so a 20-worker pool can block shutdown for over a minute and still drop the tail. After every deploy or rebalance those messages are redelivered, and any handler that is not idempotent can double-write.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

SpanFlusher.join() sets the shared stopped flag, spends the entire timeout in next_step.join(), then breaks out of the process loop when remaining_time <= 0 before calling process.terminate(). Unlike the previous single-process join, a timed-out shutdown therefore does not signal or kill any flusher process that is blocked in Redis or Kafka future.result() and has not yet observed stopped. Those processes are not reaped on rebalance (the consumer process stays up; daemon exit only happens when the parent exits), so they keep flushing the same shards while the new assignment starts its own flushers. That races flush_segments/done_flush_segments and produces duplicate segments to the buffered-segments topic.

false_positives.candidate:

SIGKILL is asynchronous, and kill failures are swallowed, so the old process can still be inside flush_segments, produce, or done_flush_segments when the replacement process starts on the same shard list. Two flushers then mutate the same Redis segments and both emit Kafka payloads, duplicating spans. The replaced Process object is also dropped without join(), so each restart leaks a zombie until the consumer exits.

Flusher metric tags embed comma-joined shard lists

shard_tag is ",".join of every shard owned by the process, and it is sent as the statsd/metrics tag shard (and, on wait_produce, shards). With the CLI default of --flusher-processes 1, one process owns every assigned partition, so the tag value is a comma-separated list such as "0,1,2,...". DogStatsD encodes tags as comma-separated key:value pairs, so that value is parsed as extra tags and the timer is dropped or attributed wrong. It also makes the series cardinality depend on the partition assignment instead of a single shard id, and the same string is set as a Sentry SDK tag that will exceed the 200-character tag limit on large assignments.

This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

false_positives.candidate:
Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure

FixedQueuePool creates each worker queue with queue.Queue() and submit() always put()s without a max size. The strategy docstring claims natural backpressure when queues fill, but an unbounded queue never blocks the Arroyo poll thread. If result handling is slower than ingest, every message is copied into process memory and the consumer keeps fetching. A slow subscription or DB stall can grow memory until the process is OOM-killed, and offsets still outstanding will be reprocessed after restart.

Kafka commits are issued from a background thread

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy starts a daemon commit thread that calls the Arroyo commit callback about once a second. That callback is only safe on the strategy thread (poll/join); it mutates consumer offset state that the processor also touches. Committing from another thread can race with poll, rebalance, and shutdown, producing incorrect commits, exceptions in the consumer, or a commit that does not match what the processor believes is safe.

Strategy close kills the factory-owned worker pool

The queue pool and its threads are created once on ResultsStrategyFactory, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() and terminate() call queue_pool.shutdown(), which sets worker.shutdown, calls Queue.shutdown(), and joins the workers. Arroyo closes the strategy on every partition revoke/rebalance and then calls create_with_partitions again on the same factory. The next strategy still holds the already-shut-down pool, so later submit() calls fail or drop work and the consumer cannot process after the first rebalance or restart of the assignment.

Submit failures are acknowledged and never retried

If decode, grouping, or queue put raises, submit() logs and immediately add_offset/complete_offset for that broker offset. The commit loop then treats the message as fully processed and commits past it. Unlike RunTask, this does not crash the consumer, retry, or DLQ. A transient error (DB blip during grouping, queue already shut down, codec glitch that escapes decode_payload) permanently skips the uptime result, so incidents derived from that check are never created.

Shutdown abandons queued work and can skip the final commit

close() stops the commit thread before pool.shutdown(). shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True and then shuts the queues down. A worker blocked in get() may process one item and then exit because the flag is set, leaving the rest of the queue unprocessed. Those offsets stay outstanding, and because the commit thread has already been joined they are never committed. join() also ignores the timeout argument and close() joins each worker for up to 5s sequentially, so a 20-worker pool can block shutdown for over a minute and still drop the tail. After every deploy or rebalance those messages are redelivered, and any handler that is not idempotent can double-write.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Block check writes match stats during validation

should_block? increments match_count and saves the row as a side effect of validation. UsersController#create calls user.valid? and then user.save, and save validates again, so a matching do_nothing row is counted twice on every successful signup attempt. The increment is also a non-atomic read-modify-write, so concurrent signups lose updates. A failed or rolled-back user save still leaves the counter changed, because the BlockedEmail write is a separate commit. Stats and last_match_at cannot be trusted, and every email validation now does an extra write.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying issue: an email-blocking check unexpectedly writes match statistics during a read/validation operation, creating concurrency risks. The candidate adds specific consequences such as double counting and lost updates.

true_positives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Domain whitelist/blacklist regex is unanchored and barely escaped

email_in_restriction_setting? only escapes dots, then matches /@(#{domains})/i anywhere in the address with no end anchor. A whitelist of example.com therefore accepts user@example.com.attacker.com (and any other string that merely contains @example.com). The same pattern makes a blacklist miss or over-match, and any other regex metacharacter in the site setting (|, +, parentheses) is interpolated live, so a bad setting raises RegexpError and turns signup validation into a 500. This is the only enforcement of those settings after the check was moved off User.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same unanchored domain regex in email_in_restriction_setting?, which allows domains containing a whitelisted domain string to bypass restrictions. The candidate uses a different exploit example and adds escaping concerns, but the underlying boundary-anchoring issue matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive and unnormalized

BlockedEmail.should_block? looks up the address with an exact equality match and never downcases or strips it. Mailbox providers treat the domain (and almost always the whole address) as case-insensitive, and signup stores whatever case the client sent (User.new_from_params assigns params[:email] raw, while change_email downcases). An attacker who is listed as blocked@evil.com can register Blocked@evil.com or " blocked@evil.com" and skip the block entirely. The unique index on blocked_emails.email has the same problem, so both casings can be stored as distinct rows.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same case-sensitive lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block? that allows differently capitalized email addresses to bypass a block. Its additional normalization and index concerns do not change the underlying match.

false_positives.candidate:
Moved domain rules and real block lookup are untested

EmailValidator is the new home of the whitelist/blacklist checks, but the spec only stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and never exercises domain settings, case folding, or a real blocked row. The old User#email_validator tests were deleted with the method, so a whitelist bypass or a block that does not fire on User save would not be caught.

true_positives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() mixin uses 0-based values for 1-based box-ordinal-group

The 2009 flexbox properties -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group are 1-based (the initial value is 1) and reject 0, while modern order and -ms-flex-order are 0-based. The mixin writes the same $val to all of them. order(1) therefore sorts with default siblings in old WebKit instead of after them, and order(0) is invalid there. Header and topic styles already call order(2) and order(3); those two happen to stay after default items, but any later order(0) or order(1) will not match modern layout in the browsers this mixin claims to prefix.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the mixin passes 0-based order values to -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group, which require values starting at 1, making order(0) invalid and causing incorrect legacy-browser layouts.

false_positives.candidate:
Small-action button no longer pins to the right

.small-action is now a flex container (display:flex plus the prefixed flexbox mixin), so the button's float:right is ignored in every browser that takes that display. The button is only a flex item with the default flex: 0 1 auto and no margin-left: auto, so it sits immediately after .small-action-desc instead of at the far edge of the row. The same change also drops the 4em left padding that used to clear the floated avatar; in browsers that do not apply flex, the avatar's float:left then overlaps the description.

Header panel alignment breaks under the prefixed flexbox the mixin enables

.panel lost float:right and now relies on margin-left:auto while .contents is turned into a flex container by the new flexbox() mixin, which emits display:-ms-flexbox and display:-webkit-box before display:flex. Those older flex models do not absorb auto margins, and once they apply, floats on flex items are ignored. In IE10 (and old WebKit that only honors the 2009 box syntax) the panel therefore stays next to the title instead of on the right. There is no float or justify-content fallback left in the rule.

extra-info-wrapper order has no flex parent

order(2) is set on .extra-info-wrapper and order(3) on .d-header .panel, but this change only makes .d-header .contents a flex container. .extra-info-wrapper is not a descendant of .contents in these styles, so it is not a flex item and order does nothing. The docked topic title will not slot between the site title and the header panel the way the order values imply; only in-flow children of .contents participate.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
website_name bypasses TL0 website hiding

include_website_name is missing the trailing ? that ActiveModel Serializers requires (every other include hook in this file is include_*?). The hook is therefore never called, so website_name is always serialized. The method also reads user_profile.website directly and is not listed in untrusted_attributes, which is what hides website from anonymous viewers of TL0 users. Those viewers now receive the website host and, when the domain heuristic matches, the path, defeating the spam/privacy restriction. The serializer spec's untrusted_attributes list was not updated, so this leak is untested.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same missing trailing '?' on include_website_name and its effect on conditional serialization. It adds a privacy-impact explanation but omits the golden comment's secondary string-literal mutation concern.

false_positives.candidate:
Invalid or non-ASCII websites disappear from the profile

website_name parses the stored website with URI and rescues every error to nil, then returns nil when host is nil. The profile template now renders the globe link only when model.website_name is present, replacing the old client split that displayed the host segment of any non-empty URL. Ruby's URI rejects non-ASCII hosts (IDN) and many user-typed URLs, so those profiles lose the website label entirely instead of falling back to the hostname. The second URI() call that appends the path is outside the rescue, so a parse failure there raises during serialization.

Domain check treats unrelated hosts as the same site

The else branch treats the website as the same site whenever Discourse.current_hostname ends with '.' plus the website host, and the elsif branch equates any two hosts that share every label after the first when they have the same label count greater than 2. That matches public suffixes and unrelated names, not just the instance domain: a site at forum.example.com will expand http://com/login to 'com/login', and http://evil.example.com/phish will be expanded the same way as a real sibling such as www. Host comparison is also case-sensitive against Discourse.current_hostname while URI#host is lowercased, so Example.com vs example.com skips the equal-host branch and omits the path the feature is supposed to show.

true_positives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
open-uri fetch of attacker-influenced URLs enables SSRF

`import_remote` does `open(url).read` with no redirect limit, timeout, or address filter, and `PollFeed` does the same for `feed_polling_url`. Embed misses enqueue `RetrieveTopic`, which calls this after only comparing `URI(embed_url).host` to `embeddable_host`. `open-uri` follows redirects, so a URL on the allowed host (or a feed entry whose link redirects) can make the app server request internal addresses such as link-local metadata endpoints. The embed referer check does not constrain where that URL ultimately connects.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies PollFeed fetching feed_polling_url with open-uri without address filtering, enabling requests to internal addresses. This matches the golden SSRF issue caused by fetching an attacker-controlled site-setting URL without validation, despite the candidate also discussing related redirect and embedding paths.

true_positives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage targetOrigin is a full referer URL, so resize never arrives

`parent.postMessage(..., '<%= request.referer %>')` passes the parent page URL, including path and query. `postMessage` requires `*` or an origin (scheme, host, port only). Browsers reject a URL with a path, so the `discourse-resize` message is never delivered and the iframe in `embed.js` stays at its default height.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same issue: passing the full referrer URL as postMessage targetOrigin instead of its origin, preventing delivery of the resize message.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Imported HTML and embed URLs are stored and rendered unsanitized

`TopicEmbed.import` appends the source URL into an HTML footer via string interpolation (`<a href='#{url}'>`) and saves the body with `cook_method: raw_html`. `Post#cook` then returns that raw string unchanged, and the embed view prints it with `raw post.cooked`. Feed items never pass through Readability or Sanitize, so script tags, event handlers, and `javascript:` URLs in RSS/Atom HTML are stored as the topic's cooked HTML and execute for every forum viewer, not just the iframe. The URL check only requires an `http(s)://` prefix, so a quote or `>` in the link/query breaks out of the footer anchor as well.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same XSS issue in TopicEmbed.import: unescaped URL interpolation into the HTML footer allows attribute breakout and injection. It does not mention the additional NoMethodError when contents is nil, but directly matches the golden comment's security concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Embed template has invalid ERB and will not render

`<%- end if %>` is not valid Ruby, so compiling `app/views/embed/best.html.erb` raises a SyntaxError. Any request that finds an existing topic and renders the best-comments iframe (the success path in EmbedController#best) fails instead of showing the discussion.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same invalid ERB closing syntax, `end if`, which causes a Ruby SyntaxError when rendering the template; the block should close with `end`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feed import crashes when an item has no content

`i.content.scrub` assumes every SimpleRSS item has a non-nil `content` string. RSS items commonly only set `description` (and Atom items can omit content), and `String#scrub` does not exist on Ruby 2.0, which this app still boots. The first such item raises NoMethodError, aborts the whole hourly poll, and also aborts TopicRetriever when it calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute` on an embed cache miss. There is no per-item rescue, so one bad entry blocks every later item.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: calling i.content.scrub when feed items lack content causes a nil-related NoMethodError, particularly when only description is provided. Its additional Ruby compatibility concern does not change this match.

false_positives.candidate:
Every embed cache miss re-imports the entire feed

When `feed_polling_enabled` is on and the embed URL is not yet stored, `perform_retrieve` runs `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute`, which downloads the feed and calls `TopicEmbed.import` for every item, synchronously inside the retrieve job. That work is already scheduled hourly, is not bounded by the 60-second per-URL Redis throttle once the job has started, and uses a blocking `open` with no timeout. A slow or large feed stalls Sidekiq and can be triggered repeatedly by embed traffic for URLs that are not in the feed.

embed_url is limited to 255 characters

`t.string :embed_url` uses the Rails default varchar(255), and `topic_id_for_embed` looks up the full URL exactly. Article and feed permalinks with long paths or tracking query strings will fail the insert (or be truncated, then never match the original `embed_url`). Those pages stay on the loading iframe and are re-fetched forever instead of embedding.

Embed controller spec expects a call the controller does not make

The success example stubs `TopicRetriever.new` and expects `retrieve`, but `EmbedController#best` only calls `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)`. As written the example fails, and nothing asserts that a job is enqueued, that `embed_url` is restricted to `embeddable_host`, or that the loading template is rendered. The poll-feed spec likewise never exercises `poll_feed` item parsing.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Second downsize definition overrides width/height API

Ruby keeps only the later `self.downsize` (line 149). The method defined at line 145, which builds a `#{max_width}x#{max_height}` geometry, is never callable. Existing callers that pass numeric width and height now hit the dimensions form, so the height integer is treated as `opts`. `opts[:allow_animation]` then raises NoMethodError, and even if that is avoided the geometry is a bare width with the height dropped. Thumbnail/downsize jobs that still use the old signature will fail or resize incorrectly.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the duplicate downsize definition: the later dimensions-string version overrides the original width/height version, making it unreachable and breaking callers using separate width and height arguments.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client size check ignores site settings

`validateUploadedFile` used to compare against `SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` and now always uses `10 * 1024`. Attachments are no longer limited by `max_attachment_size_kb`, and images are no longer limited by `max_image_size_kb`. If an admin set a limit below 10MB, the composer accepts files the server will reject; if the image limit is above 10MB, legitimate uploads are blocked client-side and the automatic downsize path never runs. The 413 handler at line 246 has the same hardcoded 10MB, so the alert text does not match the real limit.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the hardcoded 10 * 1024 limit replacing per-type site settings, causing client/server limit mismatches, and note the same problem in the 413 handler.

false_positives.candidate:
ImageMagick convert reads and writes the same tempfile

`OptimizedImage.downsize` is invoked with the upload tempfile path as both source and destination. `convert` opens the output before it finishes reading the input, so an in-place resize commonly truncates or corrupts the file (often to an empty or partial image). The upload is then stored from that same path via `Upload.create_for`, so users can lose the original and end up with a broken image instead of a downsized one. Downsize must write to a separate temp path and replace the upload file only after success.

Downsize failures are ignored and 80% geometry is wrong

The loop never checks the boolean returned by `OptimizedImage.downsize`. On failure the same file is retried until `attempt` hits 0, then `Upload.create_for` still runs. The geometry passed is `"80%"`, and `downsize_instructions` always appends `\>` (shrink-only), producing `-resize 80%\>`. ImageMagick does not treat that as a valid percentage shrink, so convert typically exits non-zero and the image is never reduced below `max_image_size_kb`. Oversized uploads therefore still fail, or a partially written file is saved.

URL downloads always capped at 10MB for every type

`FileHelper.download` previously used `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` and now always passes `10.megabytes`, before the code knows whether the URL is an image. Non-image API uploads ignore `max_attachment_size_kb` (larger attachments that the site allows are truncated/rejected at 10MB; smaller limits are not enforced here). Image URLs bigger than 10MB never reach the new downsize loop, so the feature does not cover the large remote images it is meant to shrink, and the cap cannot be configured.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unsubscribe crashes when no TopicUser exists

unsubscribe loads TopicUser with find_by and then calls tu.notification_level and tu.save! with no nil check. Users who were emailed but have no topic_users row (or whose row was removed) get a NoMethodError instead of an unsubscribe. The action should create the row (TopicUser.change / find_or_initialize) and set the level, including the notifications_changed_at / reason fields that change() normally writes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same nil dereference: when no TopicUser record exists, tu is nil and calling methods on it causes a crash. The candidate's additional remediation details do not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Unsubscribe is a state-changing GET with no token

GET /t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe immediately writes the current user's TopicUser notification level, and check_xhr is skipped so a normal browser navigation (and cross-site requests that send the session cookie) can hit it. Mail-security scanners and link prefetchers issue GETs on email links, and any site can embed the URL to mute or demote a logged-in victim's topic notifications without CSRF protection. The link in the email is exactly this URL, so opening or previewing the message can change notification state before the user chooses anything. Unsubscribe needs a non-prefetchable method (POST) and a user-bound token, or a confirmation page that does not mutate on GET.

Watching and tracking users are not actually unsubscribed

If notification_level is above regular (tracking=2 or watching=3), the action sets it to regular instead of muted. Those are the users who receive per-topic notification mail, and the new email copy says the link will stop notifications for this topic. One click only demotes them to regular, so reply, mention, and quote mail can continue. A second click is required to mute, and nothing in the email says that. The link should set muted (or whatever level truly stops topic mail) in one request.

Unsubscribe template is not resolved for the new route

The Ember route is registered as topicUnsubscribe (path /t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe), whose controller, route, and view are topic-unsubscribe. This template lives at topic/unsubscribe.hbs, which the resolver binds to a nested topic.unsubscribe route that was never defined. After the server renders the app shell, the client route has no template, so the confirmation copy and the topic-notifications-button never render. Move the template to topic-unsubscribe.hbs (or nest the route as topic.unsubscribe and point the URL there).

No tests for the unsubscribe action

The new endpoint changes notification level, redirects on slug mismatch, and is linked from every notification email, but the only spec change is passing unsubscribe_url into MessageBuilder. There is no coverage for missing TopicUser, watching vs regular vs muted, unauthenticated access, or the slug redirect. Those paths can 500 or leave the user subscribed without a failing test.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Empty updateMany cannot bump SelectedCalendar.updatedAt

fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache calls SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {}) to refresh SelectedCalendar.updatedAt after writing cache. Prisma rejects updateMany when data is empty ("data must not be empty"), and even if it did not, @updatedAt is only rewritten when some other field changes. This runs after the cache upsert, so a successful Google cache refresh still throws and the timestamp the new status UI depends on is never updated.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the empty data object passed to updateManyByCredentialId as preventing SelectedCalendar.updatedAt from updating after a cache refresh, causing inaccurate cache status tracking. The candidate adds a claim about Prisma throwing, but still identifies the same underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Env rewrite uses macOS-only sed

The new webhook helper updates GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL with sed -i '' , which is BSD/macOS syntax. On GNU sed that form treats '' as the script and does not edit the file in place, so the script reports success while leaving .env unchanged on Linux.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same portability bug: the BSD/macOS sed -i '' syntax fails on Linux with GNU sed.

false_positives.candidate:
Deleting cache does not refresh connected-calendars data

deleteCacheMutation only toasts and calls the optional onSuccess prop. Unlike the disconnect mutation in the same component, it never invalidates viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars. SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper passes onChanged through and does not refetch that query itself, so after a successful delete the dropdown still shows the old cache timestamp and "Delete cached data" until a full reload.

Cache status ignores expiry

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds groups every CalendarCache row for the credential and returns max(updatedAt) with no expiresAt >= now() filter. Expired rows still produce a cacheUpdatedAt, so CredentialActionsDropdown treats the credential as having live cache (hasCache is just a truthy timestamp) and offers delete for data the availability path will not serve.

dev:cron now depends on undeclared tsx

dev:cron was changed from ts-node (a declared devDependency of @calcom/web) to npx tsx, but tsx is not listed in this package. yarn dev:cron will download an arbitrary tsx via npx or fail offline/in CI, instead of using the previously pinned local runner.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours gate does not enforce the host's day

The new working-hours check only returns false when it finds a WorkingHours row whose days include slotStartTime.day() and whose range excludes the slot. If the fixed host has no row for that weekday, find returns nothing and the slot is treated as inside working hours. Also both start and end minutes are computed from slotStartTime, so a slot that starts inside the range and ends past workingHour.endTime is not rejected. Round-robin aggregate slots that exist because another host works that day still pass for a fixed host who does not.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that both start and end minutes are computed from slotStartTime, allowing slots ending after working hours to pass. This matches the golden issue of using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime, despite also reporting a separate weekday-check issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
All-day block override is never detected

The unavailable-all-day case is written as dayjs(start).add(offset) === dayjs(end).add(offset). Dayjs instances are never strictly equal, so this branch never runs. A date override stored with equal start and end (the usual "block this day" shape) therefore does not force the slot unavailable. Combined with the later dateOverrideExist return, that day can be treated as open instead of blocked.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify strict equality between separate Dayjs instances as the bug: === compares object references rather than date values, so the equal-date condition never succeeds. The candidate describes the resulting unavailable-day behavior, matching the golden issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Date override short-circuits busy checks

In checkIfIsAvailable, once any date override is deemed to fall on the slot's calendar day and the slot is not rejected as outside that window, the function returns true immediately. That return happens before the busy-interval loop, so bookings, calendar busy times, and buffers passed in as busy are ignored for every slot on a day that has a date override. Fixed-host and round-robin filtering both call this helper with the host's busy list, so a host can be offered (and booked) during an override window where they already have a conflict.

Any non-covering override rejects the slot

dateOverrides.find treats a callback return of true as "slot is unavailable". The callback returns true when the slot ends at or before that override's start or starts after that override's end. If a host has more than one override window on the same day (for example 09:00-10:00 and 14:00-16:00), the window that does not contain the slot makes find succeed and the function returns false, even when another window fully contains the slot. Multiple date overrides on one day, which the product supports, will hide valid slots.

Override day compare mixes local and UTC formatting

The override side is dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset).format("YYYY MM DD"), which formats in the process local timezone, while slotStartTime is time.utc() and formats in UTC. On any server whose local zone is not UTC, the same instant can format as different calendar days, so a fixed host's override is applied to the wrong day or not applied at all. Availability then depends on where the Node process is running.

Timezone offset wraps override times at midnight

Override start and end are shifted by inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset and then reduced with .hour() and .minute() only. Those accessors wrap at 00:00/24:00, so a negative or positive offset that crosses midnight turns an evening window into a morning minute-of-day (or the reverse) on the invitee's current day instead of the adjacent day. Large timezone gaps, which this change is meant to fix, still produce the wrong slots or drop the override.

New tests do not cover the stated fixes

The added assertion only re-queries a single-user event in Asia/Dhaka and expects the same UTC slot list as the IST case. true_positives.matched_candidate:

SpanFlusher.join() sets the shared stopped flag, spends the entire timeout in next_step.join(), then breaks out of the process loop when remaining_time <= 0 before calling process.terminate(). Unlike the previous single-process join, a timed-out shutdown therefore does not signal or kill any flusher process that is blocked in Redis or Kafka future.result() and has not yet observed stopped. Those processes are not reaped on rebalance (the consumer process stays up; daemon exit only happens when the parent exits), so they keep flushing the same shards while the new assignment starts its own flushers. That races flush_segments/done_flush_segments and produces duplicate segments to the buffered-segments topic.

SIGKILL is asynchronous, and kill failures are swallowed, so the old process can still be inside flush_segments, produce, or done_flush_segments when the replacement process starts on the same shard list. Two flushers then mutate the same Redis segments and both emit Kafka payloads, duplicating spans. The replaced Process object is also dropped without join(), so each restart leaks a zombie until the consumer exits.

Flusher metric tags embed comma-joined shard lists

shard_tag is ",".join of every shard owned by the process, and it is sent as the statsd/metrics tag shard (and, on wait_produce, shards). With the CLI default of --flusher-processes 1, one process owns every assigned partition, so the tag value is a comma-separated list such as "0,1,2,...". DogStatsD encodes tags as comma-separated key:value pairs, so that value is parsed as extra tags and the timer is dropped or attributed wrong. It also makes the series cardinality depend on the partition assignment instead of a single shard id, and the same string is set as a Sentry SDK tag that will exceed the 200-character tag limit on large assignments.

Signature conversion then succeeds with a value that is not the one that was signed, so verification can fail closed only by chance, or accept a rewritten component, instead of raising IOException on malformed DER.

The suite generates a single KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC") key, which is P-256, and uses it for ES256, ES384, and ES512. It only asserts that asn1derToConcatenatedRS and concatenatedRSToASN1DER round-trip through this provider's own decoder. It never calls Signature.verify on the DER produced by concatenatedRSToASN1DER, and ES384/ES512 never see 48-byte or 66-byte R/S values from a matching curve. The golden comment says AssertionError where the candidate says ValueError, but the underlying problem is the same.

The lock is now taken only to assign b.cache[key]. getOrCreateIndex still does check-then-act (GetIndex, then build) with no per-key singleflight, and init can build many namespaces at once. Two callers for the same NamespacedResource can both pass GetIndex, both call bleve.New on the same directory (file indexes fail or corrupt the on-disk index), and the last cache write wins while the other caller keeps using the orphaned index. Searches and watch updates then diverge.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same issue: the cacheMu lock now covers only the cache assignment instead of the whole BuildIndex, so concurrent builds of the same key can race.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
