TotalDocs ranges over b.cache with no cacheMu held, while BuildIndex writes that map under cacheMu. searchSupport.init now starts the watch goroutine (which can BuildIndex a namespace that was below the init threshold) and then calls TotalDocs for the new startup log. A concurrent map write during that iteration panics the process.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same race. TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization while the watcher goroutine started in init can call BuildIndex and write the map at the same time, risking a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
Concurrent index init races on shared err

searchSupport.init launches one errgroup goroutine per namespace and each one does `_, _, err = s.build(...)` plus `totalBatchesIndexed++` on variables declared outside the loop. Those are unsynchronized shared writes. With BuildIndex no longer holding a process-wide lock, these goroutines actually run together, so a failed build can have its error overwritten by a later successful one (startup proceeds with a missing index) or a finished success can be overwritten by another goroutine's error (startup fails spuriously). The counter read for the trace event is likewise racy.

Failed constructor Init leaks lifecycle and in-flight builds

NewResourceServer now calls s.Init and, on error, returns nil without s.cancel() or lifecycle.Stop. Init runs lifecycle.Init (SQL backend opens the DB) before search.init. If index build fails, the caller has no server handle to stop the backend, so the DB pool is leaked. The cancelable context passed into the errgroup is also dropped, so in-flight namespace builds keep running after the constructor has already failed. Previously Init errors were returned on the live server, which could still be stopped.

Search watch loop panics when the event channel closes

After the index build, init always starts `for { v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v) }` on context.Background(), not the server context. WatchWriteEvents' poller closes that channel when the SQL backend is stopped. A receive on a closed channel yields a nil *WrittenEvent, and handleEvent immediately reads evt.Type, which panics. Because init now runs inside NewResourceServer, every storage server starts this goroutine, and shutdown (server.Stop / backend cancel) will crash it. The goroutine also cannot be cancelled independently of the SQL poller.

TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer is the integration test that constructs and runs a storage-server target, which now builds the unified index inside NewResourceServer/InitializeModuleServer. The change skips that test whenever GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres, with a TODO that it fails in Drone. Postgres startup regressions from eager index init (the failure mode this PR is fixing) will not be caught in CI.

The PR's stated trace fix is to pass the span context into child work (`ctx, span := tracer.Start`). BuildIndex, which this change edits, still does `_, span := b.tracer.Start(...)`. The builder callback and SQL list work started from the incoming ctx are not children of the BuildIndex span, so the index-build trace stays disconnected from the work it wraps.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure

FixedQueuePool creates each worker queue with queue.Queue() and submit() always put()s without a max size. The strategy docstring claims natural backpressure when queues fill, but an unbounded queue never blocks the Arroyo poll thread. If result handling is slower than ingest, every message is copied into process memory and the consumer keeps fetching. A slow subscription or DB stall can grow memory until the process is OOM-killed, and offsets still outstanding will be reprocessed after restart.

Kafka commits are issued from a background thread

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy starts a daemon commit thread that calls the Arroyo commit callback about once a second. That callback is only safe on the strategy thread (poll/join); it mutates consumer offset state that the processor also touches. Committing from another thread can race with poll, rebalance, and shutdown, producing incorrect commits, exceptions in the consumer, or a commit that does not match what the processor believes is safe.

Strategy close kills the factory-owned worker pool

The queue pool and its threads are created once on ResultsStrategyFactory, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() and terminate() call queue_pool.shutdown(), which sets worker.shutdown, calls Queue.shutdown(), and joins the workers. Arroyo closes the strategy on every partition revoke/rebalance and then calls create_with_partitions again on the same factory. The next strategy still holds the already-shut-down pool, so later submit() calls fail or drop work and the consumer cannot process after the first rebalance or restart of the assignment.

Submit failures are acknowledged and never retried

If decode, grouping, or queue put raises, submit() logs and immediately add_offset/complete_offset for that broker offset. The commit loop then treats the message as fully processed and commits past it. Unlike RunTask, this does not crash the consumer, retry, or DLQ. A transient error (DB blip during grouping, queue already shut down, codec glitch that escapes decode_payload) permanently skips the uptime result, so incidents derived from that check are never created.

Shutdown abandons queued work and can skip the final commit

close() stops the commit thread before pool.shutdown(). shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True and then shuts the queues down. A worker blocked in get() may process one item and then exit because the flag is set, leaving the rest of the queue unprocessed. Those offsets stay outstanding, and because the commit thread has already been joined they are never committed. join() also ignores the timeout argument and close() joins each worker for up to 5s sequentially, so a 20-worker pool can block shutdown for over a minute and still drop the tail. After every deploy or rebalance those messages are redelivered, and any handler that is not idempotent can double-write.

Queue-depth test races the workers

test_stats_reporting submits 10 items and immediately asserts get_stats()["total_items"] > 0. Workers are already running and the processor is a no-op, so the queues can be empty before that assertion. The test will flake under load even though the pool is behaving correctly. The same pattern does not wait until in-flight work finishes: qsize() is 0 as soon as a worker has dequeued an item, so wait_until_empty can return while processing is still running.

GetWebAssets snapshots entryPointAssetsCache under a read lock, drops that lock, and only then takes the write lock and always reloads and assigns entryPointAssetsCache. Two callers that both observe a nil cache can both enter the write section. If the first finishes and publishes a good manifest, the second still overwrites it—including with nil when its read fails—so a successful fill is discarded and later non-dev callers miss the cache or all redo the load. After Lock, re-read the cache and return it when non-nil and not in dev, and do not assign a failed result over an existing entry.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same flaw: the cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock, which breaks the double-checked locking in GetWebAssets.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker shortened from 10 minutes to 1 minute

Run now starts the background cleanup ticker at 1 minute instead of 10. Nothing in the PR description or the deadlock fix requires this, and it looks like leftover debugging next to the new Error logs. clean() uses a 9-minute timeout and runs synchronously, while time.Ticker buffers one tick, so a job longer than a minute will be re-entered immediately and the whole cleanup suite (annotations, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, invites, short URLs, query history) can run nearly continuously. That copies the whole string each iteration. The new integration test exercises this path with a batch of 32767, so a single DELETE statement build is quadratic in the batch size and can stall the cleanup goroutine for a large annotation table. true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Storage failures and legacy delete-collection are recorded on the wrong metric series

On Storage.Create failure the code calls recordLegacyDuration (line 45) instead of recordStorageDuration; Storage.Update failure does the same at line 129. Successful Delete records the object name as the kind label (line 106: recordStorageDuration(..., name, ...)) instead of options.Kind, so the kind cardinality is object names. The legacy DeleteCollection goroutine calls recordStorageDuration (line 166) rather than recordLegacyDuration, so legacy latency and errors are attributed to unified storage. Mode 3 dashboards and alerts will mis-attribute failures and cannot tell whether the safety write succeeded.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly notes that the successful Delete passes the object name as the kind label to recordStorageDuration instead of options.Kind. That is the same inconsistency the golden comment describes, even though the candidate also raises other metric-series issues.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled when the handler returns

Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine via context.WithTimeoutCause on the incoming request context (lines 51, 110, 135, and 163). That child context is cancelled as soon as the apiserver finishes the request and cancels the parent, which is normally before the 10s timeout. The legacy write that mode 3 is supposed to perform as a safety copy therefore fails immediately with context canceled, so legacy storage silently diverges from unified storage.

Legacy create/update replay the caller's object instead of the unified result

After Storage.Create returns, the goroutine calls Legacy.Create with the same obj pointer the storage implementation just mutated (UID, resourceVersion, timestamps). Legacy.Update (line 139) likewise reuses the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of writing the object Storage.Update already produced. The previous mode 3 update path wrapped that result so both stores stored the same bytes. Legacy optimistic concurrency then sees the unified resourceVersion, rejects or no-ops the write, and the two stores diverge. Failures are not logged, only counted, so the mismatch is invisible.

Mode 3 unit tests mock the wrong store and never wait for the legacy goroutine

The create/update/delete error cases set expectations on Legacy (or none on Storage) even though the implementation returns the Storage error and only then calls Legacy. An unmocked Storage.Create returns a nil error, so the wantErr cases do not exercise the path they name. Success cases start an unsynchronized goroutine that calls Legacy after the test function returns and never assert that the legacy call happened or that its error was recorded. These tests will flake or panic on the mock after the test ends and do not lock in the dual-write contract.

Mode 3 playlist integration test reads legacy immediately after an async write

The new mode 3 file/unified/etcd cases call doPlaylistTests, which creates, updates, and deletes through the Kubernetes API and then immediately lists and gets the same objects on the legacy /api/playlists endpoints (around lines 522-531 and getFromBothAPIs). Mode 3 only copies to legacy asynchronously and does not wait for that copy, so those assertions race the goroutine and will flake or fail even when the async write would eventually succeed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Pause is never offered in the ruler-less list

The list view now computes canPause from Grafana Prometheus abilities because ruler rules are no longer loaded, but the Pause item is still gated on rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule). GrafanaRuleListItem only passes promRule, so rulerRule is undefined and Pause stays hidden for every Grafana-managed rule even when the user is allowed to pause it.

canDelete is OR-ed with the new Prometheus ability so list-view permissions can allow deletion, but the Delete menu item is still rendered only when rulerRule is truthy. The new list never supplies a ruler rule, so users with delete permission cannot delete a Grafana rule from the list. The group-loader menu test also encodes this by expecting four items and omitting Delete despite granting AlertingRuleDelete.

Federated rules are no longer treated as immutable

useAllAlertRuleAbilities used to set isFederated from isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) before deciding edit, delete, pause, and duplicate support. The refactor hardcodes isFederated to false and forwards every combined rule through useAllRulerRuleAbilities. Federated cloud rule groups, which this helper still serves outside the list view, can now be edited or deleted even though federation makes them immutable.

Rule view links drop the return path

The removed list item built the view href with createReturnTo() so leaving a filtered or grouped list could navigate back to that list. The new href is only /alerting/grafana/${uid}/view. Opening a rule from the list no longer preserves the list URL, so the rule view's back/return navigation lands somewhere other than the list the user came from.

$__range queries are interpolated before the no-split check

runSplitQuery now runs datasource.applyTemplateVariables on every target before querySupportsSplitting. That helper refuses to split expressions that still contain $__range, because the variable must be interpolated against each split window (the comment on querySupportsSplitting says backend interpolation of the split range is required). Template replacement consumes $__range using request.scopedVars for the full original range, so the check then sees a plain duration and splits the query anyway. Each chunk is executed with the full-range duration already baked in, so range-variable queries return wrong series. The $__range check has to happen on the raw expression, and $__range must not be replaced until each sub-range is known.

Shard splitting interpolates, then runSplitQuery interpolates again

runShardSplitQuery maps every target through applyTemplateVariables, then splitQueriesByStreamShard always delegates execution to runSplitQuery, which applies applyTemplateVariables a second time (the updated test even expects 5 calls for a single target). applyTemplateVariables also appends request.filters as ad-hoc matchers. The second pass therefore duplicates those matchers on an already rewritten expr, producing invalid or overly constrained LogQL and wrong results whenever ad-hoc filters are set. Interpolation for the shard path should happen once, and the inner runSplitQuery call must not template-replace targets that are already interpolated.

Empty-after-interpolation queries are no longer dropped

Previously interpolateVariablesInQueries ran before the expr/hide filters, so a target whose expression was only a variable that resolved to "" was removed and never queried. The new code filters on the raw expr first and only then calls applyTemplateVariables. A target like expr: "$query" that interpolates to an empty string now stays in the shard groups and is sent to Loki, which errors or returns unintended results. Filter again after interpolation, the same way the old interpolate-then-filter order did.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check is not atomic with insert

CreateOrUpdateDevice counts active rows and, only if count < deviceLimit, runs a separate INSERT. Those steps are not in one transaction and take no lock, so concurrent anonymous logins can all observe the same count below the cap and all insert. The configured limit can be exceeded under parallel traffic (multiple Grafana instances make this worse). Enforce the cap in the same transaction as the insert, or with a row/advisory lock, so the count and write cannot race.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same race condition: the non-atomic count check followed by an insert lets concurrent requests exceed the device limit. Both suggest a transaction or lock as the fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device-limit denial is cached, so a retry bypasses the limit

tagDeviceUI writes the device key into localCache before CreateOrUpdateDevice returns. When the store rejects a new device with ErrDeviceLimitReached, that key stays cached for the default 29 minutes and the error is returned only for the current call. Authenticate treats that error as a hard failure, but the next anonymous request for the same X-Grafana-Device-Id hits the cache, returns nil, and is issued an anonymous identity without ever being inserted or counted. Refreshing once therefore bypasses the configured device limit, and those sessions never appear in the 30-day count, so the cap stays artificially low. Clear the cache entry (or set it only after a successful write) when tagging fails.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same bug: the cache is set before CreateOrUpdateDevice, so after ErrDeviceLimitReached the entry persists for 29 minutes and later requests bypass the device limit.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locale files are not loaded on translate

The on-demand loader in translate only calls load_locale for I18n.config.locale, and load_translations was patched to never load other locale YAML files. FallbackLocaleList therefore only works when something has already called I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!, which this PR does solely from ApplicationController#set_locale. Mailers, Sidekiq/jobs, the console, and any I18n.with_locale / I18n.locale= path never load the site-default or English files, so a missing key in the active locale stays missing instead of falling back. Server-side fallbacks are broken for most non-request translation.

Translation cache ignores dynamic fallback locale

The accelerator cache key is only key + current locale + backend object id. Fallback resolution now depends on SiteSetting.default_locale, which can change at runtime without replacing the backend. After an admin changes the site default locale, cached hits keep the translation resolved through the old fallback chain (or a previously cached missing result) until that LRU entry is evicted, so users see the wrong language for keys that are not defined in their own locale.

No tests for custom fallback chain or preload

FallbackLocaleList and the ensure_loaded! hook are new behavior with no specs. Nothing checks the user-locale → site default → :en order, that fallback YAML is actually loaded before lookup, or that translations outside ApplicationController#set_locale still fall back. The loader/cache bugs above would not be caught before merge.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

true_positives.golden_comment: In the next action, capping the next offset at user_count can produce an empty page (e.g., total equal to limit results in offset == total, showing 2/2 with no members). This can cause confusing UX on the last page.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
totalPages is one too high when count is a multiple of limit

totalPages is Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1. When user_count is an exact multiple of limit (50 members, limit 50) that is 2 instead of 1. showingLast stays false on the real last page, so Next is enabled. next then sets offset to user_count and findMembers loads an empty extra page. Use ceil(user_count / limit), and treat a zero count as zero pages.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug. When the total is a multiple of the limit, Next stays enabled and sets the offset to user_count, which loads an empty extra page. The candidate pins the root cause on the totalPages calculation, while the golden comment points at the next-action cap. The symptom is identical.

true_positives.golden_comment: The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Automatic-group remove spec uses PUT and never hits the route

The example "cannot remove members from automatic groups" calls xhr :put, :remove_member, while the route is DELETE /admin/groups/:id/members and the success example correctly uses :delete. Controller specs invoke the action by name and inject group_id, so this never checks routing or that params[:id] is what the action reads. That is why the group_id vs :id mismatch is untested. The members action's new {members, meta} contract also has no spec.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point out that the remove_member test uses xhr :put while the route requires DELETE. The candidate also raises extra issues, but the core problem is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `totalPages` calculation using `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` produces an extra page when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`, leading to incorrect pagination. For example, with 100 users and a limit of 50, it reports 3 pages instead of 2, allowing navigation to an empty page.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
totalPages is one too high when count is a multiple of limit

totalPages is Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1. When user_count is an exact multiple of limit (50 members, limit 50) that is 2 instead of 1. showingLast stays false on the real last page, so Next is enabled. next then sets offset to user_count and findMembers loads an empty extra page. true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same bug: totalPages is computed as Math.floor(user_count/limit)+1, which gives one page too many when the count is an exact multiple of the limit. That extra page lets the user navigate to an empty page. The candidate adds more detail but describes the same issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Add/remove members reads group_id but the route supplies id

add_members and remove_member both do Group.find(params.require(:group_id)). The new routes are member routes on resources :groups (DELETE/PUT /admin/groups/:id/members), so Rails populates params[:id], not params[:group_id]. The client only puts the id in the path (/admin/groups/:id/members.json) and sends usernames or user_id in the body. params.require(:group_id) therefore raises ParameterMissing and every add or remove from the admin UI returns 400. Controller specs hide this by passing group_id directly and never hitting the router.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: the route supplies params[:id], but the code reads params[:group_id], so the group membership actions fail. The candidate is more detailed but identifies the same mismatch.

false_positives.candidate:
Creating a group drops alias_level

create only assigns name and visible. The admin form shows the alias-level combo for new groups, and Group#asJSON posts alias_level on POST /admin/groups, but the action never reads it. A group created with anything other than the default alias level (for example everyone / 99) is saved as the default, and the choice is silently lost. update does apply alias_level, so the field only works after the group already exists.

Remove control ignores automatic groups

The member row is an itemView whose context is the user, not the group, so {{#unless automatic}} does not see the group's automatic flag. The flag is always falsy on the user, so the remove link is rendered for automatic groups (trust levels, staff, and so on). The server rejects those deletes with 422, and removeMember never surfaces the error, so the confirm dialog appears to succeed and the member stays. The add-members block in group.hbs correctly hides itself; this row does not.

Removing the last member on a page leaves a blank page

removeMember reloads with the current offset and does not move back a page when that page becomes empty. The members action echoes the requested offset and does not clamp it to the new total. After deleting the last user on a page, the response has members: [] while offset is still past the new user_count. The client stores that offset, so the admin stays on a blank page until they click Previous. findMembers only clamps offset against the stale user_count from before the delete.

Members limit and offset are not bounded

limit is (params[:limit] || 50).to_i and offset is params[:offset].to_i with no upper or lower bound, on a public endpoint that now paginates every group including large automatic ones. A caller can pass limit of millions or a negative limit/offset. limit(0) is also echoed back to the admin client, which then divides user_count by that limit and produces Infinity/NaN page numbers. Clamp limit to a small positive maximum (and offset to >= 0) before querying.

GET group members response shape changed without a compatibility path

GET /groups/:id/members used to render a JSON array of users via GroupUserSerializer. It now returns {members, meta}. Any plugin, theme, or external client that still treats the body as an array will break. The in-repo templates were updated, but nothing in this PR versions the endpoint or keeps the old array format.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Block check writes match stats during validation

should_block? increments match_count and saves the row as a side effect of validation. UsersController#create calls user.valid? and then user.save, and save validates again, so a matching do_nothing row is counted twice on every successful signup attempt. The increment is also a non-atomic read-modify-write, so concurrent signups lose updates. A failed or rolled-back user save still leaves the counter changed, because the BlockedEmail write is a separate commit. Stats and last_match_at cannot be trusted, and every email validation now does an extra write.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same flaw: the block-check method updates match statistics as a side effect of what should be a read-only check. The candidate also raises race conditions from the non-atomic increment, which the golden comment mentions too.

true_positives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Domain whitelist/blacklist regex is unanchored and barely escaped

email_in_restriction_setting? only escapes dots, then matches /@(#{domains})/i anywhere in the address with no end anchor. A whitelist of example.com therefore accepts user@example.com.attacker.com (and any other string that merely contains @example.com). The same pattern makes a blacklist miss or over-match, and any other regex metacharacter in the site setting (|, +, parentheses) is interpolated live, so a bad setting raises RegexpError and turns signup validation into a 500. This is the only enforcement of those settings after the check was moved off User.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same flaw: the improperly anchored regex @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? lets a whitelist be bypassed. The golden example is a subdomain-style bypass (evil.example.com). The candidate's example is a suffix bypass (example.com.attacker.com). Both stem from missing anchoring in the same regex, so it is essentially the same issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive and unnormalized

BlockedEmail.should_block? looks up the address with an exact equality match and never downcases or strips it. Mailbox providers treat the domain (and almost always the whole address) as case-insensitive, and signup stores whatever case the client sent (User.new_from_params assigns params[:email] raw, while change_email downcases). An attacker who is listed as blocked@evil.com can register Blocked@evil.com or " blocked@evil.com" and skip the block entirely. The unique index on blocked_emails.email has the same problem, so both casings can be stored as distinct rows.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem: the case-sensitive lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block? lets a differently-cased address get past a block.

false_positives.candidate:
Moved domain rules and real block lookup are untested

EmailValidator is the new home of the whitelist/blacklist checks, but the spec only stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and never exercises domain settings, case folding, or a real blocked row. The old User#email_validator tests were deleted with the method, so a whitelist bypass or a block that does not fire on User save would not be caught.

true_positives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Header panel alignment breaks under the prefixed flexbox the mixin enables

.panel lost float:right and now relies on margin-left:auto while .contents is turned into a flex container by the new flexbox() mixin, which emits display:-ms-flexbox and display:-webkit-box before display:flex. Those older flex models do not absorb auto margins, and once they apply, floats on flex items are ignored. In IE10 (and old WebKit that only honors the 2009 box syntax) the panel therefore stays next to the title instead of on the right. There is no float or justify-content fallback left in the rule.
true_positives.reasoning: Both flag the removal of float:right on .panel breaking right alignment, but in different contexts: golden is the non-flex noscript header, candidate is old prefixed flexbox ignoring auto margins. Same code change, different mechanism; borderline partial match.

true_positives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() mixin uses 0-based values for 1-based box-ordinal-group

The 2009 flexbox properties -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group are 1-based (the initial value is 1) and reject 0, while modern order and -ms-flex-order are 0-based. The mixin writes the same $val to all of them. order(1) therefore sorts with default siblings in old WebKit instead of after them, and order(0) is invalid there. Header and topic styles already call order(2) and order(3); those two happen to stay after default items, but any later order(0) or order(1) will not match modern layout in the browsers this mixin claims to prefix.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. The 2009 box-ordinal-group properties are 1-based, but the mixin passes the same 0-based value to them, so a value of 0 is invalid and old browsers render the layout incorrectly.

false_positives.candidate:
Small-action button no longer pins to the right

.small-action is now a flex container (display:flex plus the prefixed flexbox mixin), so the button's float:right is ignored in every browser that takes that display. The button is only a flex item with the default flex: 0 1 auto and no margin-left: auto, so it sits immediately after .small-action-desc instead of at the far edge of the row. The same change also drops the 4em left padding that used to clear the floated avatar; in browsers that do not apply flex, the avatar's float:left then overlaps the description.

extra-info-wrapper order has no flex parent

order(2) is set on .extra-info-wrapper and order(3) on .d-header .panel, but this change only makes .d-header .contents a flex container. .extra-info-wrapper is not a descendant of .contents in these styles, so it is not a flex item and order does nothing. The docked topic title will not slot between the site title and the header panel the way the order values imply; only in-flow children of .contents participate.

false_negatives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
website_name bypasses TL0 website hiding

include_website_name is missing the trailing ? that ActiveModel Serializers requires (every other include hook in this file is include_*?). The hook is therefore never called, so website_name is always serialized. The method also reads user_profile.website directly and is not listed in untrusted_attributes, which is what hides website from anonymous viewers of TL0 users. Those viewers now receive the website host and, when the domain heuristic matches, the path, defeating the spam/privacy restriction. The serializer spec's untrusted_attributes list was not updated, so this leak is untested.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that include_website_name is missing the trailing '?', so the conditional inclusion hook is not used. The candidate does not mention the string mutation point, but the core missing-'?' issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Invalid or non-ASCII websites disappear from the profile

website_name parses the stored website with URI and rescues every error to nil, then returns nil when host is nil. The profile template now renders the globe link only when model.website_name is present, replacing the old client split that displayed the host segment of any non-empty URL. Ruby's URI rejects non-ASCII hosts (IDN) and many user-typed URLs, so those profiles lose the website label entirely instead of falling back to the hostname. The second URI() call that appends the path is outside the rescue, so a parse failure there raises during serialization.

Domain check treats unrelated hosts as the same site

The else branch treats the website as the same site whenever Discourse.current_hostname ends with '.' plus the website host, and the elsif branch equates any two hosts that share every label after the first when they have the same label count greater than 2. That matches public suffixes and unrelated names, not just the instance domain: a site at forum.example.com will expand http://com/login to 'com/login', and http://evil.example.com/phish will be expanded the same way as a real sibling such as www. Host comparison is also case-sensitive against Discourse.current_hostname while URI#host is lowercased, so Example.com vs example.com skips the equal-host branch and omits the path the feature is supposed to show.

true_positives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
open-uri fetch of attacker-influenced URLs enables SSRF

`import_remote` does `open(url).read` with no redirect limit, timeout, or address filter, and `PollFeed` does the same for `feed_polling_url`. Embed misses enqueue `RetrieveTopic`, which calls this after only comparing `URI(embed_url).host` to `embeddable_host`. `open-uri` follows redirects, so a URL on the allowed host (or a feed entry whose link redirects) can make the app server request internal addresses such as link-local metadata endpoints. The embed referer check does not constrain where that URL ultimately connects.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly says PollFeed calls open() on feed_polling_url without filtering, which enables SSRF. That is the same issue as the golden comment, even though the candidate also covers import_remote.

true_positives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage targetOrigin is a full referer URL, so resize never arrives

`parent.postMessage(..., '<%= request.referer %>')` passes the parent page URL, including path and query. `postMessage` requires `*` or an origin (scheme, host, port only). Browsers reject a URL with a path, so the `discourse-resize` message is never delivered and the iframe in `embed.js` stays at its default height.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem: postMessage is given the full referrer URL as targetOrigin when it needs only the origin. As a result the message is dropped and the iframe resize fails.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Imported HTML and embed URLs are stored and rendered unsanitized

`TopicEmbed.import` appends the source URL into an HTML footer via string interpolation (`<a href='#{url}'>`) and saves the body with `cook_method: raw_html`. `Post#cook` then returns that raw string unchanged, and the embed view prints it with `raw post.cooked`. Feed items never pass through Readability or Sanitize, so script tags, event handlers, and `javascript:` URLs in RSS/Atom HTML are stored as the topic's cooked HTML and execute for every forum viewer, not just the iframe. The URL check only requires an `http(s)://` prefix, so a quote or `>` in the link/query breaks out of the footer anchor as well.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment raises two issues: a nil contents NoMethodError and an XSS from unescaped url interpolation. The candidate explicitly covers the XSS from the url interpolated into the footer anchor, which is a substantial part of the golden comment. It does not mention the nil contents issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Embed template has invalid ERB and will not render

`<%- end if %>` is not valid Ruby, so compiling `app/views/embed/best.html.erb` raises a SyntaxError. Any request that finds an existing topic and renders the best-comments iframe (the success path in EmbedController#best) fails instead of showing the discussion.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same bug: the `end if` in the ERB template is invalid Ruby and makes rendering fail.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feed import crashes when an item has no content

`i.content.scrub` assumes every SimpleRSS item has a non-nil `content` string. RSS items commonly only set `description` (and Atom items can omit content), and `String#scrub` does not exist on Ruby 2.0, which this app still boots. The first such item raises NoMethodError, aborts the whole hourly poll, and also aborts TopicRetriever when it calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute` on an embed cache miss. There is no per-item rescue, so one bad entry blocks every later item.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say `i.content.scrub` assumes content is non-nil, while many RSS items only provide description, so a nil content crashes the import. The candidate adds extra points, but the core issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Every embed cache miss re-imports the entire feed

When `feed_polling_enabled` is on and the embed URL is not yet stored, `perform_retrieve` runs `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute`, which downloads the feed and calls `TopicEmbed.import` for every item, synchronously inside the retrieve job. That work is already scheduled hourly, is not bounded by the 60-second per-URL Redis throttle once the job has started, and uses a blocking `open` with no timeout. A slow or large feed stalls Sidekiq and can be triggered repeatedly by embed traffic for URLs that are not in the feed.

embed_url is limited to 255 characters

`t.string :embed_url` uses the Rails default varchar(255), and `topic_id_for_embed` looks up the full URL exactly. Article and feed permalinks with long paths or tracking query strings will fail the insert (or be truncated, then never match the original `embed_url`). Those pages stay on the loading iframe and are re-fetched forever instead of embedding.

Embed controller spec expects a call the controller does not make

The success example stubs `TopicRetriever.new` and expects `retrieve`, but `EmbedController#best` only calls `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)`. As written the example fails, and nothing asserts that a job is enqueued, that `embed_url` is restricted to `embeddable_host`, or that the loading template is rendered. The poll-feed spec likewise never exercises `poll_feed` item parsing.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Second downsize definition overrides width/height API

Ruby keeps only the later `self.downsize` (line 149). The method defined at line 145, which builds a `#{max_width}x#{max_height}` geometry, is never callable. Existing callers that pass numeric width and height now hit the dimensions form, so the height integer is treated as `opts`. `opts[:allow_animation]` then raises NoMethodError, and even if that is avoided the geometry is a bare width with the height dropped. Thumbnail/downsize jobs that still use the old signature will fail or resize incorrectly.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. The downsize method is defined twice, and the later dimensions-string version overrides the width/height version. This leaves the original unreachable and breaks existing callers that pass width and height separately.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client size check ignores site settings

`validateUploadedFile` used to compare against `SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` and now always uses `10 * 1024`. Attachments are no longer limited by `max_attachment_size_kb`, and images are no longer limited by `max_image_size_kb`. If an admin set a limit below 10MB, the composer accepts files the server will reject; if the image limit is above 10MB, legitimate uploads are blocked client-side and the automatic downsize path never runs. The 413 handler at line 246 has the same hardcoded 10MB, so the alert text does not match the real limit.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same problem: the hardcoded 10MB limit replaces the per-type SiteSettings, so the client-side limit can diverge from the server-side one. Both also note that the 413 handler has the same hardcoded value.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Downsize failures are ignored and 80% geometry is wrong

The loop never checks the boolean returned by `OptimizedImage.downsize`. On failure the same file is retried until `attempt` hits 0, then `Upload.create_for` still runs. The geometry passed is `"80%"`, and `downsize_instructions` always appends `\>` (shrink-only), producing `-resize 80%\>`. ImageMagick does not treat that as a valid percentage shrink, so convert typically exits non-zero and the image is never reduced below `max_image_size_kb`. Oversized uploads therefore still fail, or a partially written file is saved.
true_positives.reasoning: Both flag the '80%' geometry as invalid and causing downsize to silently fail. The golden issue is specifically about gifsicle --resize-fit on animated GIFs; the candidate attributes the failure to ImageMagick's '\>' handling. Same parameter and symptom, different root cause.

false_positives.candidate:
ImageMagick convert reads and writes the same tempfile

`OptimizedImage.downsize` is invoked with the upload tempfile path as both source and destination. `convert` opens the output before it finishes reading the input, so an in-place resize commonly truncates or corrupts the file (often to an empty or partial image). The upload is then stored from that same path via `Upload.create_for`, so users can lose the original and end up with a broken image instead of a downsized one. Downsize must write to a separate temp path and replace the upload file only after success.

URL downloads always capped at 10MB for every type

`FileHelper.download` previously used `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` and now always passes `10.megabytes`, before the code knows whether the URL is an image. Non-image API uploads ignore `max_attachment_size_kb` (larger attachments that the site allows are truncated/rejected at 10MB; smaller limits are not enforced here). Fixed-host and round-robin filtering both call this helper with the host's busy list, so a host can be offered (and booked) during an override window where they already have a conflict.

If a host has more than one override window on the same day (for example 09:00-10:00 and 14:00-16:00), the window that does not contain the slot makes find succeed and the function returns false, even when another window fully contains the slot. The override side is dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset).format("YYYY MM DD"), which formats in the process local timezone, while slotStartTime is time.utc() and formats in UTC. true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.

Unlike sendScheduledEmails, sendLocationChangeEmails, and the other booking mailers, it never consults eventType metadata disableStandardEmails for host or attendee. true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same problem: sendAddGuestsEmails never checks the eventType metadata disableStandardEmails flags. As a result, hosts and attendees receive emails even when standard emails are disabled.

false_positives.candidate:
Any attendee can add guests; host restrictions ignored

Authorization succeeds for any logged-in user whose email matches an attendee on the booking, with no check that the event type allows guests (disableGuests) and no check that the booking is accepted and upcoming. A booker (or a compromised attendee account) can therefore append arbitrary emails, persist them as attendees, and have the meeting details—including videoCallData url/password—emailed to those addresses, bypassing the booker-side guest disable setting. The mutation is also unbounded: ZAddGuestsInputSchema does not cap guests.length, so one call can create and email a very large attendee list.

Calendar update uses the caller's credentials, not the host's

updateCalendarAttendees is invoked with an EventManager built from ctx.user and getUsersCredentials(ctx.user). The booking query already loads booking.user.credentials and destinationCalendar, but those are never passed to EventManager. The organizer's connected calendar is not updated, and the caller's own calendar may be written instead, so the new attendees never appear on the host event (or the wrong calendar is mutated).

Seated bookings get raw attendee rows, not seats

Guests are inserted with attendees.createMany and the handler copies seatsPerTimeSlot onto the calendar event but never creates BookingSeat / seat-reference rows or checks remaining capacity. On a seated event type, attendance is tracked via seats, not free-form attendees. This can overfill the slot, omit the new people from seat-based emails and cancellation, and leave attendee rows that the seats UI does not treat as booked seats.

true_positives.golden_comment: Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

Codes are 10 hex characters (0-9a-f) and the login UI placeholder is "XXXXX-XXXXX", which leads users and mobile keyboards to enter uppercase. The same check in apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts (line 61) has the same bug. Legitimate backup codes will be rejected at login and when disabling 2FA. true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
A backup code can be redeemed twice under concurrent logins

Consumption is a read-modify-write: decrypt the list, indexOf the code, set that slot to null, then update. Two overlapping authorize calls can both observe the same unused code and both return a session before either write lands. The product promise is that each code works exactly once. The update needs to be conditional (transaction or compare-and-swap on the stored ciphertext) so a code that was already removed cannot authorize a second session.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same race condition: the read-modify-write on decrypted backup codes lets concurrent logins reuse a single code, which breaks one-time use.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup-code login skips the password when any totpCode is sent

Password verification runs only when credentials.totpCode is empty (line 121). The new branch then accepts a matching backup code and never checks the TOTP value. A caller who knows the email and one backup code can therefore sign in with no password by also sending any non-empty totpCode (for example "000000"). The UI copy and the login form still treat the backup code as a replacement for the authenticator only, after the password step, so this is an account takeover path if a backup code leaks (downloaded file, clipboard, setup response). Require a valid password for CAL users on the backup-code path, and do not let a dummy totpCode bypass that check.

Lost-access toggle submits the disable form

The Lost access / Go back control is a Button inside the disable Form with no type="button" and no preventDefault. A button's default type is submit, so clicking it both flips the backup-code view and posts whatever is currently in the password/TOTP/backup fields. That can disable 2FA accidentally, or fail the request and show an incorrect-code error, instead of only switching inputs. Set type="button" (same issue on the download control in EnableTwoFactorModal, which sits inside the enable Form and will also submit handleEnable).

Enable-2FA login test never leaves the backup-code step

After a successful OTP, EnableTwoFactorModal now stays open on the backup-code step and only calls onEnable when backup-codes-close is clicked. This test still waits for the security-page switch and asserts it is checked without closing that dialog. The second test was updated to click close; this one was not, so it will fail or pass only because of the existing isChecked() quirk noted in the FIXME. It also never exercises login or disable with a backup code (the new TODO), so the feature this PR adds is untested.

Missing-backup-codes message points at a settings action that does not exist

missing_backup_codes tells the user to generate codes in settings. This PR only creates codes during 2FA setup and clears them on disable; there is no regenerate control. Users who enabled 2FA before the migration have backupCodes null and will see this error on Lost access, with no way to follow the instruction except fully disabling and re-enabling 2FA. The string should describe that actual path.

Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.

Calendar/video cleanup is not awaited on reschedule

Reschedule therefore marks the booking cancelled, sends the reschedule email, and returns true while calendar deleteEvent / deleteMeeting are still in flight. On a serverless runtime the process can freeze before those calls finish, so the old calendar event and meeting are left behind and failures become unhandled rejections.

false_positives.candidate:
Calendar/video cleanup is not awaited on reschedule

Same as the vital reschedule path: await getCalendar was added inside bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...). The caller never waits for those promises, so cancellation of the previous calendar event and video meeting races the email send and the function return. Errors from getCalendar or deleteEvent are not caught by the try/catch, and a short-lived request can exit before the external events are actually deleted.

Recurring calendar deletes are pushed after the await set is already consumed

When cancelling all remaining occurrences, credentials are walked with forEach(async ...) and getCalendar is awaited before calendar.deleteEvent. The resulting promises are pushed onto apiDeletes only after that await. Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes)) later in the handler therefore often runs while apiDeletes is still empty, so those deletes are not part of the awaited set. The handler can return, and a serverless isolate can exit, before recurring calendar events are removed.

Every app import() starts immediately and can reject unhandled

Each import() is invoked while evaluating the appStore object, so loading this module starts every app package at once and does not load an app only when it is used. A rejection is only handled if some caller later awaits that specific key. Any app whose promise rejects before it is awaited (failed module, missing dependency) is an unhandled rejection and can crash the Node process, even for a request that never touches that app.
